parole.significato: abbreviation (shortened or contracted form of a word or phrase)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian abbreviatura, from Late Latin abbrevio (“to shorten”).
Borrowed from Italian avaria, from Arabic عَوَارِيَّة (ʕawāriyya, “damaged goods”), from عَوَار (ʕawār, “fault, blemish, defect, flaw”), from عَوِرَ (ʕawira, “to lose an eye”).
Borrowed from Italian adagio, perhaps through French adagio, based on the pronunciation.

parole.significato: arpeggio (notes of a chord played individually)
an artel: a worker or peasant cooperative.
parole.testo: Unknown or disputed: borrowed from Italian artiere or from Turkish or Uralic.
From Northern Italian articiocco, from Provençal archichaut, arquichaut, from Old Spanish alcarchofa, from Andalusian Arabic الْخَرْشُوف (al-ḵaršūf), from Arabic الْخُرْشُوف (al-ḵuršūf).
Derived from Italian arcipelago, from Ancient Greek ἀρχι- (arkhi-) + πέλαγος (pélagos).

parole.significato: barista (person who prepares coffee in a coffee shop for customers)

parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian basta or Spanish basta.
Borrowed from Italian battaglia or French bataille.
Borrowed from Italian baule, from Turkic.

First recorded in the 1st Pskov manuscript. Often used in the 17th century. Inherited from Old East Slavic башта (bašta) from Italian bastia via Polish baszta or Czech bašta. The ending was influenced by the suffix -ня (-nja), which creates nouns of place, as in па́шня (pášnja), тамо́жня (tamóžnja).

Borrowed from Italian belladonna (bella donna, literally “beautiful lady”), altered by folk etymology from Medieval Latin bladona (“nightshade”), from Gaulish *blātōnā, blātunā, from Proto-Celtic *blātus (“flower”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰléh₃tus, from *bʰleh₃- (“blossom, flower”). The folk ety
Alteration of брат (brat), influenced by Italian fratello.

parole.significato: bruschetta (grilled bread rubbed with garlic and topped with olive oil and salt)

parole.testo: Analyzable as бума́га (bumága) + -ный (-nyj). Vasmer hypothesizes that бума́га (bumága) might be a back-formation, and бума́жный (bumážnyj) the original term derived from Italian bambagino (“made of cotton wool”).

parole.significato: currency (money or other item used to facilitate transactions)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian valuta (“currency”), from Latin valeō (“to be worth”).
Borrowed from Italian vermicelli (“little worms”), from verme (“worm”), from Latin vermis (“worm”). Via PIE cognate with Old East Slavic вермие (vermije), English worm.
Borrowed from Italian vira, second-person singular imperative of virare.
Borrowed from Italian gondola, from Venetan góndoła, probably from Byzantine Greek κοντούρα (kontoúra, “small tail”).
Borrowed from Italian diva (“diva, goddess”), from Latin dīva (“goddess”), feminine of dīvus (“divine, divine one; notably a deified mortal”).

Borrowed from Italian duce (“leader”). Further from Latin dux (akin to dūcō), whence also дож (dož) and дюк (djuk). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dewk-, whence also the second component of ге́рцог (gércog).

parole.significato: zhupan (a style of jerkin in Poland and Ukraine)
parole.testo: From Italian giuppone, from Arabic جُبَّة (jubba). Doublet of зипу́н (zipún), шу́ба (šúba), and ю́бка (júbka). Also doublet of дже́мпер (džémper).

parole.significato: impresario (a manager or producer in the entertainment industry)
money collector, collection agent, cash messenger
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian incassare (“to collect cash, put in a box”). Omitting several steps, from Latin capsa.

parole.significato: A romantic and attractive man who is popular among women.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian casanova, named after Italian adventurer Giacomo Casanova (1725–1798).
Omitting several steps, from Italian caserma (“barracks”), via Polish kazarma or older German Kasarme.
Borrowed from Italian casino via French. Further from Latin casa.
Ultimately from Italian camiciola via Kamisol or camisole.
Possibly via Italian canfora, from Latin camphora, from Arabic كَافُور (kāfūr).
Borrowed from Italian canaglia. Further from Latin canis.
Borrowed from Italian cane corso (literally “Corsican dog”), with adjective corso being more likely derived from Latin cohors (“farmyard; enclosure”).

parole.significato: choir of singers (from the 18th century, mixed ensemble of singers and musicians)
picture (representation of visible reality produced by drawing, etc.)

parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian cassa, from Latin capsa. Doublet of ка́псула (kápsula), ка́псюль (kápsjulʹ), кассе́та (kasséta), and шасси́ (šassí).
Borrowed from Italian conservatorio. Compare Ukrainian консервато́рія (konservatórija), Belarusian кансервато́рыя (kansjervatóryja).

parole.significato: confetti (small pieces of colored paper generally thrown about at festive occasions)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian confetti, plural for confetto, via French confetti, which affected the word stress.

parole.significato: concert (musical entertainment in which several voices or instruments take part)
parole.testo: Borrowed in the 17th century from Italian concerto.
Borrowed from Italian crescendo, from Latin crēscendum.
Borrowed from Italian chianti, after Chianti, its area of production. Through Latin from the Etruscan 𐌂𐌋𐌀𐌍𐌕𐌄 (clante).
Borrowed from Italian libretto, diminutive of libro.
Borrowed from Italian lira, from Latin libra.

From Italian Lombardia (“Lombardy”). In the Medieval period Lombardy was known for its banks and usury. Compare natively formed Bulgarian заложна къща (založna kăšta), Czech zastavárna, Macedonian заложилница (založilnica), Serbo-Croatian залагаоница.
Borrowed from Italian mafiosi, plural of mafioso.
Borrowed from Italian maestro. Further from Latin magister. Doublet of маги́стр (magístr), ма́стер (máster), ми́стер (míster), and мэтр (mɛtr).
Borrowed from Italian mi, from Latin mīra, the first word of the third line of Ut queant laxis, the medieval hymn which solfège was based on.
Borrowed from Italian mosaico, from Medieval Latin musaicum.
Borrowed from Italian paparazzi, plural of paparazzo.
From Italian patina, from Latin patina (“dish, pan”).
Perhaps borrowed from Italian plastilina. For sense 2, compare with English usage of plasticine for "Palestine" in Internet slang.
Borrowed from Italian pomi d'oro, plural of pomo d'oro, archaic form of pomodoro.
Borrowed from Italian prima donna (“first lady”).
Borrowed from Italian Prosecco. Doublet of про́сека (próseka).
Derived from Italian radice, but via one or more intermediaries, judging by the first vowel. Further from Latin rādīx.
Borrowed from Italian salto (“jump”). Further from Latin saltus (saliō + -tus).

parole.significato: salto mortale (a dangerous and daring jump with possibly lethal outcome)
sirocco (hot and humid southeast to southwest wind)

parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian sonata, from Latin sonare.
Borrowed from Italian soffitto (“ceiling”). Further from Latin suffīgō (sub- + Latin fīgō), compare Latin suffīxus.
Borrowed from Italian sparagio, from Latin asparagus, from Ancient Greek ἀσπάραγος (aspáragos).

parole.significato: modeling tool (wooden, bone or metal tool for sculpting clay or similar soft material, with a wide, blade-like end)

parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian studio. Compare Belarusian сту́дыя (stúdyja) and Ukrainian сту́дія (stúdija).
Borrowed from Italian tariffa, ultimately from Arabic تَعْرِيف (taʕrīf).

parole.significato: stencil (utensil consisting of a perforated sheet)

parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian fagotto, perhaps via German Fagott.
Borrowed from Italian fiasco. Doublet of флако́н (flakón) and фля́жка (fljážka).

parole.significato: finita la commedia, “the comedy is over”, (said when something abruptly ends or is cancelled)

parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian fora, a variant of fuori.

parole.significato: citadel (a strong fortress that sits high above a city)
parole.testo: From Italian cittadella, via Polish cytadela.

parole.significato: socle (plinth, i.e. thickened bottom part of a wall or pedestal, often used to display art work)
parole.testo: Formerly цо́коло (cókolo) (in the time of Peter the Great); borrowed from Italian zoccolo, from Latin socculus, diminutive of soccus.
Borrowed from Italian zucchini, plural of zucchino.
Originally чокола́д (čokolád) and чикола́д (čikolád), borrowed from Italian cioccolata. The form шокола́д (šokolád) was borrowed from German Schokolade.
From штукату́р(ить) (štukatúr(itʹ)) + -ка (-ka), ultimately from Italian stuccatura.
Borrowed from Italian abbate, or Middle High German abbāt, from Latin abbās (“abbot”), oblique stem abbat-. Further (via Ancient Greek ἀββα (abba) and Aramaic אבא) from Proto-Semitic *ʔabw-.

parole.significato: to put (a proposal) to a vote
parole.testo: From German ballot(ieren) + -и́ровать (-írovatʹ) or from French balloter + -и́ровать (-írovatʹ), from Italian ballottare (“to vote with balls”), from Italian ballotta (“ball”).

Borrowed in the second half of 18th century (first attested in 1785, form барказ (barkaz) in 1762) from Dutch barkas (“a large or the largest row-boat on a ship”) (att. since 1718), Swedish barkasse (since 1765) or possibly another Western European language, from some Romance language. Compare Itali

parole.significato: grandiose (large and impressive, in size, scope or extent)
parole.testo: Per Shansky, probably an adapted borrowing of French grandiose + -ный (-nyj). Per Vasmer, from either German grandios or Italian grandioso. Compare Ukrainian грандіо́зний (hrandióznyj), Belarusian грандыёзны (hrandyjózny).
Borrowed from French girafe, German Giraffe or Italian giraffa.
Borrowed from French girafe, German Giraffe or Italian giraffa.
Attested 1698. Borrowed from Polish kawaler or German Kavalier, from French cavalier, from Italian cavaliere.
Borrowed from French carton or from German Karton, both borrowed from Italian cartone.

parole.significato: coffee (in the form of a beverage)
parole.testo: First attested in late 17th or early 18th century. Borrowed from a West Germanic language, either English coffee, German Koffee, or directly from Dutch koffie, Ultimately from Italian caffè, from Arabic قَهْوَة (qahwa). Doublet of кафе́ (kafé).
Borrowed from Italian mecenate or from German Mäzenat, ultimately from Latin Maecēnās.

Inherited from Old East Slavic скоморохъ (skomoroxŭ), of unknown origin. Possibly from Ancient Greek σκώμμαρχος (skṓmmarkhos, “joke leader”) (σκῶμμα (skômma)+ἀρχός (arkhós)) or from Italian scaramuccia.
